---
title: Render modes
questions:
  - id: static-ssr
    prompt: A component with no render mode in a Blazor Web App renders with static server-side rendering. What does that mean?
    options:
      - id: html-only
        text: The server renders HTML once per request; `@onclick` handlers do not run
        correct: true
      - text: It runs in WebAssembly after the page loads
      - text: It keeps a SignalR circuit open
      - text: It cannot use any C# code
    explanation: Static SSR produces plain HTML. Interactivity requires an interactive render mode; forms and links can still work through enhanced navigation and form posts.
  - id: auto
    prompt: How does the `InteractiveAuto` render mode decide how to run a component?
    options:
      - text: It always uses WebAssembly
      - id: auto-choice
        text: It uses Interactive Server while the WebAssembly runtime is not yet available, and WebAssembly once it can be loaded quickly
        correct: true
      - text: It asks the user to choose
      - text: It switches back and forth on every click
    explanation: Auto gives fast first interaction via the server, then moves to client-side execution on later visits once assets are cached. A component keeps its chosen mode once it starts.
  - id: prerender
    prompt: How do you disable prerendering for an interactive server component?
    options:
      - text: Add `@prerender false` to the component
      - text: Prerendering cannot be disabled
      - id: new-mode
        text: "`@rendermode @(new InteractiveServerRenderMode(prerender: false))`"
        correct: true
    explanation: Each interactive render mode class takes a `prerender` argument; prerendering is on by default.
  - id: rules
    prompt: Which statements about render modes are true?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Interactive WebAssembly and Auto components must be in an assembly the browser can download, usually the `.Client` project
        correct: true
      - text: Parameters passed from a static parent to an interactive child must be serializable
        correct: true
      - text: A child of an interactive component inherits its parent's render mode
        correct: true
      - text: A child of an Interactive Server component can switch itself to Interactive WebAssembly
    explanation: Render mode flows down the tree and cannot be switched to a different interactive mode inside an interactive subtree.
---
## Learning objectives

- Describe the four render modes
- Apply render modes per component, per page or globally
- Understand prerendering and the rules for mixing modes

## The four modes

| Mode | Where it runs | Interactive | Notes |
|------|---------------|-------------|-------|
| Static SSR | Server, per request | No | Fast, SEO-friendly HTML |
| `InteractiveServer` | Server, over a SignalR circuit | Yes | Tiny download; needs a constant connection |
| `InteractiveWebAssembly` | Browser | Yes | Works offline after download; larger first load |
| `InteractiveAuto` | Server first, then browser | Yes | Best of both, more moving parts |

## Applying a render mode

```razor
@page "/counter"
@rendermode InteractiveServer
```

```razor
<Counter @rendermode="InteractiveWebAssembly" />
```

Make an entire app interactive by setting the mode on the root `Routes` and `HeadOutlet`
components in `App.razor`:

```razor
<HeadOutlet @rendermode="InteractiveAuto" />
<Routes @rendermode="InteractiveAuto" />
```

## Prerendering

Interactive components are **prerendered** on the server by default: the user sees HTML
immediately, then the component becomes interactive. Lifecycle methods therefore run twice — once
during prerender and once when interactive — which matters for data loading (see the state
chapter).

## Knowing where you are

.NET 9 added `RendererInfo` and `AssignedRenderMode`:

```razor
@if (!RendererInfo.IsInteractive)
{
    <p>Loading interactive features…</p>
}
<button disabled="@(!RendererInfo.IsInteractive)" @onclick="Save">Save</button>

<small>Running on: @RendererInfo.Name</small>
```

`RendererInfo.Name` is `Static`, `Server`, `WebAssembly` or `WebView`. Disabling buttons until
interactive prevents clicks that would do nothing during prerendering.

## Rules for mixing modes

- Interactive modes flow **down** the component tree
- A child cannot switch to a *different* interactive mode
- Parameters from a static parent to an interactive child must be JSON-serializable — so you
  cannot pass `RenderFragment` child content across that boundary
- WebAssembly/Auto components must live where the browser can download them

  - id: two-projects

    options:

      - text: Because Razor files cannot be in the server project
      - id: download

  - id: program
    prompt: Which calls are needed in the server's `Program.cs` to support Interactive Server components?
    type: multiple
    options:

        correct: true
      - text: "`app.UseAntiforgery()`"

## Learning objectives

- Create a Blazor Web App from the template
- Understand the server and client projects
- Read the `Program.cs` that wires render modes together

## Creating the app

```bash
dotnet new blazor -n Shop --interactivity Auto
```

| Option | Values |
|--------|--------|
| `--interactivity` | `None`, `Server`, `WebAssembly`, `Auto` |
| `--all-interactive` | Make the whole app interactive instead of per page |
| `--auth` | `None` or `Individual` |

## Solution layout

```text
Shop/                    server project (ASP.NET Core)
  Components/
    App.razor            root HTML document
    Routes.razor         router
    Layout/
    Pages/               static or server-interactive pages
  Program.cs
Shop.Client/             WebAssembly project
  Pages/                 pages that can run in the browser
  Program.cs
```

## Server Program.cs

```csharp
var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services.AddRazorComponents()
    .AddInteractiveServerComponents()
    .AddInteractiveWebAssemblyComponents();

var app = builder.Build();

app.UseHttpsRedirection();
app.UseAntiforgery();
app.MapStaticAssets();

app.MapRazorComponents<App>()
    .AddInteractiveServerRenderMode()
    .AddInteractiveWebAssemblyRenderMode()
    .AddAdditionalAssemblies(typeof(Shop.Client._Imports).Assembly);

app.Run();
```

`MapStaticAssets` (.NET 9+) serves static files with build-time compression and fingerprinting.

## Client Program.cs

```csharp
var builder = WebAssemblyHostBuilder.CreateDefault(args);
builder.Services.AddScoped<ICartService, ClientCartService>();
await builder.Build().RunAsync();
```

Services used by components that may run in **both** places must be registered in **both**
`Program.cs` files — often with different implementations. That idea is the key to reusable
Blazor components and is covered in the data chapter.

## _Imports.razor

```razor
@using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Web
@using static Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Web.RenderMode
```

The static import is what lets you write `@rendermode InteractiveServer` instead of
`RenderMode.InteractiveServer`.

## Learning objectives

- Read and write Razor component syntax
- Split markup and code with partial classes
- Inject services and use common directives

## Anatomy

```razor
@page "/orders/{Id:int}"
@inject IOrderService Orders
@implements IDisposable

<PageTitle>Order @Id</PageTitle>

@if (order is null)
{
    <p>Loading…</p>
}
else
{
    <h1>Order @order.Number</h1>
    <ul>
        @foreach (var line in order.Lines)
        {
            <li @key="line.Sku">@line.Quantity × @line.Name</li>
        }
    </ul>
}

@code {
    [Parameter] public int Id { get; set; }
    private OrderDetails? order;

    protected override async Task OnParametersSetAsync() => order = await Orders.GetAsync(Id);

    public void Dispose() { }
}
```

## Common directives

| Directive | Purpose |
|-----------|---------|
| `@page` | Route template |
| `@rendermode` | Render mode for this component |
| `@inject` | Inject a service |
| `@using` / `@namespace` | Namespaces |
| `@implements` / `@inherits` | Interfaces and base class |
| `@typeparam` | Generic component type parameter |
| `@attribute` | Apply a C# attribute, e.g. `[Authorize]` |
| `@layout` | Choose a layout |

## Code-behind

```csharp
// OrderPage.razor.cs
public partial class OrderPage(IOrderService orders)
{
    [Parameter] public int Id { get; set; }
    private OrderDetails? order;

    protected override async Task OnParametersSetAsync() => order = await orders.GetAsync(Id);
}
```

Constructor injection in components is supported from .NET 9. Code-behind keeps large components
navigable and lets you unit test logic more easily.

## Razor expressions

- `@value` — implicit expression; HTML-encoded output
- `@(a + b)` — explicit expression
- `@((MarkupString)html)` — render trusted raw HTML (never untrusted input)
- `@* comment *@` — Razor comment, not sent to the browser

---
title: Parameters, events and data binding
questions:
  - id: eventcallback
    prompt: Why should child components expose events as `EventCallback` rather than `Action`?
    options:
      - id: rerender
        text: "`EventCallback` invokes the handler on the right component and automatically re-renders the parent afterwards, and supports async handlers"
        correct: true
      - text: "`Action` cannot be used in Razor files"
      - text: "`EventCallback` is faster because it uses reflection"
    explanation: With a plain `Action`, the parent's state changes but it does not know to re-render.
  - id: two-way
    prompt: To support `@bind-Value` on a custom component, which members must it expose?
    options:
      - text: Only a `[Parameter] public string Value { get; set; }`
      - text: "A `[Parameter] public string Bind { get; set; }`"
      - id: value-changed
        text: A `[Parameter] Value` property and a `[Parameter] EventCallback<T> ValueChanged`
        correct: true
    explanation: "`@bind-Value` expands to setting `Value` and handling `ValueChanged`. An optional `ValueExpression` supports validation in forms."
  - id: dont-mutate
    prompt: Why should a component avoid writing to its own `[Parameter]` properties?
    options:
      - text: It causes a compile error
      - text: Parameters are read-only at runtime
      - id: overwritten
        text: The parent may re-render and overwrite the value, discarding the child's changes
        correct: true
    explanation: Parameters are owned by the parent. Copy into private state or raise an event so the parent updates the value.
  - id: bind-modifiers
    prompt: Which binding features are available in Blazor?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: "`@bind:event=\"oninput\"` to update on every keystroke"
        correct: true
      - text: "`@bind:after` to run a method after the bound value changes"
        correct: true
      - text: "`@bind:get` and `@bind:set` to separate reading and writing the value"
        correct: true
      - text: "`@bind:sql` to save the value directly to a database"
    explanation: Bind modifiers customise when and how binding happens.
---
## Learning objectives

- Pass data down with parameters
- Raise events up with `EventCallback`
- Implement two-way binding on your own components

## Parameters

```razor
@* Rating.razor *@
<div class="rating" aria-label="@Value out of @Max stars">
    @for (var i = 1; i <= Max; i++)
    {
        var star = i;
        <button type="button" class="@(star <= Value ? "on" : "off")" @onclick="() => SelectAsync(star)">★</button>
    }
</div>

@code {
    [Parameter, EditorRequired] public int Value { get; set; }
    [Parameter] public EventCallback<int> ValueChanged { get; set; }
    [Parameter] public int Max { get; set; } = 5;

    private Task SelectAsync(int star) => ValueChanged.InvokeAsync(star);
}
```

`[EditorRequired]` makes the compiler warn when a parent forgets the parameter. Note the `var star = i;`
copy: the lambda must capture the loop value, not the loop variable.

## Two-way binding

```razor
<Rating @bind-Value="review.Stars" />
<p>You chose @review.Stars stars.</p>
```

`@bind-Value` expands to `Value="review.Stars"` plus `ValueChanged="v => review.Stars = v"`.

## Binding to inputs

```razor
<input @bind="search" @bind:event="oninput" @bind:after="SearchAsync" />

<input @bind:get="quantity" @bind:set="SetQuantity" type="number" />

@code {
    private string search = "";
    private int quantity = 1;

    private Task SearchAsync() => results.LoadAsync(search);
    private void SetQuantity(int value) => quantity = Math.Clamp(value, 1, 99);
}
```

## Events

```razor
<button @onclick="SaveAsync" @onclick:preventDefault>Save</button>
<input @onkeydown="OnKeyDown" />

@code {
    private async Task SaveAsync(MouseEventArgs e) { /* ... */ }
    private void OnKeyDown(KeyboardEventArgs e)
    {
        if (e.Key == "Escape") Close();
    }
}
```

Handlers can be sync or async. After an event handler completes, Blazor re-renders the component
automatically; for async handlers it renders once when the first `await` yields and again when it finishes.

title: Lifecycle and rendering
questions:
  - id: order
    prompt: In which order do these lifecycle methods first run for a new component?
    options:
      - text: OnAfterRender, OnInitialized, OnParametersSet
      - text: OnParametersSet, SetParametersAsync, OnInitialized, OnAfterRender
      - text: OnInitialized, OnAfterRender, OnParametersSet
      - id: correct-order
        text: SetParametersAsync, OnInitialized, OnParametersSet, OnAfterRender
        correct: true
    explanation: Parameters are set, then initialization runs once, then parameter processing, then rendering and finally after-render callbacks.
  - id: statehaschanged
    prompt: When do you need to call `StateHasChanged()` manually?
    options:
      - text: After every event handler
      - text: At the end of `OnInitializedAsync`
      - id: external
        text: When state changes outside Blazor's own event handling, such as from a timer or a service event
        correct: true
    explanation: Blazor re-renders after its own events and lifecycle methods. For external triggers, call `InvokeAsync(StateHasChanged)`.
  - id: key
    prompt: What does the `@key` directive do in a list?
    options:
      - id: identity
        text: Tells the diffing algorithm which rendered element or component corresponds to which data item, preserving them correctly when the list changes
        correct: true
      - text: Encrypts the element
      - text: Sets the HTML `id` attribute
    explanation: Without `@key`, Blazor matches by position, which can reuse the wrong component instance (and its state) after inserts or reorders.
  - id: render-facts
    prompt: Which statements about Blazor rendering are true?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Blazor builds a render tree and applies only the differences to the DOM
        correct: true
      - text: Overriding `ShouldRender` to return false can skip unnecessary renders
        correct: true
      - text: "`OnAfterRenderAsync(bool firstRender)` is the right place to call JavaScript that needs rendered elements"
        correct: true
      - text: "`OnAfterRender` runs during static server-side rendering"
    explanation: After-render callbacks only run for interactive components, because static SSR has no live DOM on the server.
---
## Learning objectives

- Know the order and purpose of lifecycle methods
- Trigger re-renders correctly
- Use `@key` and `ShouldRender` to control rendering

## The lifecycle

1. `SetParametersAsync` — parameters arrive
2. `OnInitialized{Async}` — first time only
3. `OnParametersSet{Async}` — first time and whenever the parent passes new parameters
4. Render
5. `OnAfterRender{Async}(firstRender)` — DOM updated (interactive only)
6. `Dispose` / `DisposeAsync` — removed from the tree

```razor
@implements IAsyncDisposable
@inject IJSRuntime JS

<div @ref="chartHost"></div>

@code {
    [Parameter] public IReadOnlyList<Point> Data { get; set; } = [];
    private ElementReference chartHost;
    private IJSObjectReference? module;

    protected override async Task OnAfterRenderAsync(bool firstRender)
    {
        if (firstRender)
        {
            module = await JS.InvokeAsync<IJSObjectReference>("import", "./Components/Chart.razor.js");
        }
        if (module is not null)
        {
            await module.InvokeVoidAsync("draw", chartHost, Data);
        }
    }

    public async ValueTask DisposeAsync()
    {
        if (module is not null)
        {
            try { await module.DisposeAsync(); } catch (JSDisconnectedException) { }
        }
    }
}
```

## Re-rendering from outside

```csharp
protected override void OnInitialized() => cart.Changed += OnCartChanged;

private void OnCartChanged() => _ = InvokeAsync(StateHasChanged);

public void Dispose() => cart.Changed -= OnCartChanged;
```

`InvokeAsync` marshals onto the renderer's synchronization context — essential in Interactive
Server, where the event may arrive on another thread. Always unsubscribe to avoid memory leaks.

## Diffing and @key

```razor
@foreach (var todo in todos)
{
    <TodoItem @key="todo.Id" Item="todo" />
}
```

## Skipping renders

```csharp
private int lastVersion = -1;

protected override bool ShouldRender()
{
    var changed = Data.Version != lastVersion;
    lastVersion = Data.Version;
    return changed;
}
```

Use `ShouldRender` only for measured hot spots; most components render quickly enough.

title: Templated and generic components
questions:
  - id: childcontent
    prompt: What is special about a parameter named `ChildContent` of type `RenderFragment`?
    options:

        correct: true
      - text: It must be set in code, never in markup
      - text: It is rendered before the component's own markup
      - text: It can only contain plain text
    explanation: By convention, `ChildContent` receives the component's inner content without an explicit tag.
  - id: render-fragment-t
    prompt: What does `RenderFragment<TItem>` allow?
    options:
      - text: Rendering only items of type `string`
      - id: template
        text: A template that receives a value — for example, how to render each row of a list
        correct: true
      - text: Running a fragment on a background thread
    explanation: The caller supplies markup that uses `context` (or a named `Context`) to access the item.
  - id: typeparam
    prompt: Which statements about generic components are true?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: "`@typeparam TItem` declares a type parameter"
        correct: true
      - text: The type argument can often be inferred from a parameter such as `Items`
        correct: true
      - text: "Constraints can be added, for example `@typeparam TItem where TItem : notnull`"
        correct: true

Reusable components separate **what** to render (the caller's business) from **how** to lay it
out (the component's business).

## Learning objectives

- Accept child content with `RenderFragment`
- Accept item templates with `RenderFragment<T>`
- Build generic components with `@typeparam`

## Child content

```razor
@* Card.razor *@
<section class="card">
    <header>@Header</header>
    <div class="card-body">@ChildContent</div>
</section>

@code {
    [Parameter] public RenderFragment? Header { get; set; }
    [Parameter] public RenderFragment? ChildContent { get; set; }
}
```

```razor
<Card>
    <Header><h2>Shipping</h2></Header>
    <ChildContent><p>Arrives in 2–3 days.</p></ChildContent>
</Card>

<Card>
    <p>Only child content — no tag needed.</p>
</Card>
```

## A generic, templated list

```razor
@* ItemList.razor *@
@typeparam TItem where TItem : notnull

@if (Items.Count == 0)
{
    @Empty
}
else
{
    <ul class="item-list">
        @foreach (var item in Items)
        {
            <li @key="item">@ItemTemplate(item)</li>
        }
    </ul>
}

@code {
    [Parameter, EditorRequired] public IReadOnlyList<TItem> Items { get; set; } = [];
    [Parameter, EditorRequired] public RenderFragment<TItem> ItemTemplate { get; set; } = default!;
    [Parameter] public RenderFragment Empty { get; set; } = @<p>Nothing here yet.</p>;
}
```

```razor
<ItemList Items="products" Context="product">
    <ItemTemplate>
        <strong>@product.Name</strong> — @product.Price.ToString("C")
    </ItemTemplate>
</ItemList>
```

`TItem` is inferred as `Product` from `Items`. `Context="product"` renames the implicit `context`
variable. The same `ItemList` now renders customers, orders or anything else.

## Fragments in C#

```csharp
private RenderFragment Badge(string text) => @<span class="badge">@text</span>;
```

Razor templates (`@<tag>...</tag>`) can be written inline in `@code` blocks to produce fragments.

title: Cascading values and shared state
questions:
  - id: cascading
    prompt: What does a `CascadingValue` provide?
    options:
      - text: A value that is stored in the browser's local storage
      - text: A global static variable shared by all users
      - id: descendants
        text: A value available to every descendant component that declares a matching `[CascadingParameter]`
        correct: true
      - text: A CSS variable
    explanation: Cascading values avoid passing the same parameter through every level of the tree.
  - id: isfixed
    prompt: "What does `IsFixed=\"true\"` on a `CascadingValue` do?"
    options:

        correct: true
      - text: Makes the value read-only for descendants
      - text: Pins the component to the top of the page
    explanation: Fixed cascading values are cheaper because descendants are not re-rendered when the cascading component re-renders.
  - id: state-container
    prompt: Which statements about a scoped "state container" service are true?
    type: multiple
    options:

        correct: true
      - text: Components should subscribe to its change event and unsubscribe when disposed

    explanation: Singletons on the server are shared by every user, so they must never hold per-user state.

## Learning objectives

- Share values down the tree with cascading values
- Register root-level cascading values
- Share state across components with a state container service

## Cascading values

```razor
<CascadingValue Value="theme" IsFixed="true">
    @Body
</CascadingValue>
```

```razor
@code {
    [CascadingParameter] public Theme Theme { get; set; } = default!;
}
```

Since .NET 8, cascading values can be registered at the root, which works across render-mode
boundaries where a `CascadingValue` component in a static layout could not reach:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddCascadingValue(sp => new Theme { Accent = "teal" });
builder.Services.AddCascadingAuthenticationState();
```

## A state container

```csharp
public sealed class CartState
{
    private readonly List<CartLine> _lines = [];
    public IReadOnlyList<CartLine> Lines => _lines;
    public decimal Total => _lines.Sum(l => l.Price * l.Quantity);
    public event Action? Changed;

    public void Add(Product product)
    {
        var line = _lines.FirstOrDefault(l => l.Sku == product.Sku);
        if (line is null) _lines.Add(new CartLine(product.Sku, product.Name, product.Price, 1));
        else line.Quantity++;
        Changed?.Invoke();
    }
}

builder.Services.AddScoped<CartState>();
```

```razor
@implements IDisposable
@inject CartState Cart

<span class="cart-badge">@Cart.Lines.Count</span>

@code {
    protected override void OnInitialized() => Cart.Changed += OnChanged;
    private void OnChanged() => InvokeAsync(StateHasChanged);
    public void Dispose() => Cart.Changed -= OnChanged;
}
```

## Where the state lives

| Host | Scoped service lifetime |
|------|-------------------------|
| Interactive Server | The user's circuit |
| WebAssembly | The app instance in that browser tab |
| Static SSR | A single HTTP request |

State in memory disappears on refresh. Persist anything important — to the server through an API,
or to browser storage (see the interop section).

title: Razor class libraries, CSS isolation and attribute splatting

        correct: true

  - id: static-path

    options:
      - id: content
        text: "`_content/Contoso.UI/logo.svg`"
        correct: true
      - text: "`/logo.svg`"
      - text: "`/Contoso.UI/wwwroot/logo.svg`"
    explanation: Static web assets from libraries are exposed under `_content/{PackageId}/`.
  - id: css-isolation
    prompt: Which statements about CSS isolation are true?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Styles in `Button.razor.css` apply only to the `Button` component's markup
        correct: true
      - text: "`::deep` lets a parent's isolated styles reach elements rendered by child components"
        correct: true
      - text: Isolated styles are bundled into a `{AssemblyName}.styles.css` file
        correct: true
      - text: Isolated styles are applied at runtime by JavaScript
    explanation: Scoping happens at build time by rewriting selectors with a unique attribute.
  - id: splatting
    prompt: What does `[Parameter(CaptureUnmatchedValues = true)]` on a dictionary parameter enable?
    options:
      - id: splat
        text: Collecting any extra attributes the caller sets, so they can be applied to an element with `@attributes`
        correct: true
      - text: Capturing exceptions thrown by children
      - text: Capturing user keystrokes
    explanation: Attribute splatting lets wrapper components pass through `id`, `aria-*`, `class` and other attributes they did not explicitly declare.
---
## Learning objectives

- Build a reusable component library
- Style components with CSS isolation
- Pass through arbitrary attributes with splatting

## Creating a library

```bash
dotnet new razorclasslib -n Contoso.UI
dotnet add Shop reference Contoso.UI
```

Add `@using Contoso.UI` to `_Imports.razor` and the components are available everywhere.

## A design-system button

```razor
@* Contoso.UI/Button.razor *@
<button type="@Type" class="cx-btn cx-btn-@Variant @Class" @attributes="AdditionalAttributes" @onclick="OnClick">
    @ChildContent
</button>

@code {
    [Parameter] public string Variant { get; set; } = "primary";
    [Parameter] public string Type { get; set; } = "button";
    [Parameter] public string? Class { get; set; }
    [Parameter] public RenderFragment? ChildContent { get; set; }
    [Parameter] public EventCallback<MouseEventArgs> OnClick { get; set; }
    [Parameter(CaptureUnmatchedValues = true)] public IReadOnlyDictionary<string, object>? AdditionalAttributes { get; set; }
}
```

```razor
<Button Variant="danger" aria-label="Delete order" title="Delete" OnClick="DeleteAsync">Delete</Button>
```

`aria-label` and `title` are not parameters, so they land in `AdditionalAttributes` and are splatted
onto the `<button>`.

## CSS isolation

```css
/* Button.razor.css */
.cx-btn { border-radius: .5rem; padding: .5rem 1rem; }
.cx-btn-danger { background: #b91c1c; color: white; }
```

At build time, selectors are rewritten with a unique attribute such as `b-3xxtam6d07`, and all
isolated CSS is bundled into `Contoso.UI.bundle.scp.css`, which flows into the consuming app's
`{AssemblyName}.styles.css`. Reference it once in `App.razor`:

```html
<link rel="stylesheet" href="@Assets["Shop.styles.css"]" />
```

Use `::deep` to style child components from a parent:

```css
.card ::deep h2 { margin-top: 0; }
```

## Static assets

Files in the library's `wwwroot` are served from `_content/Contoso.UI/...`:

```html
<img src="_content/Contoso.UI/logo.svg" alt="Contoso" />
```

## Reuse across hosts

Keep RCL components free of host-specific services. Depend on interfaces (`IProductService`) that
each host implements, and the same library works in a Blazor Web App, standalone WebAssembly and a
MAUI Hybrid app.

title: Dynamic components and error boundaries
questions:
  - id: dynamic
    prompt: When is `DynamicComponent` useful?
    options:
      - text: To render components faster
      - id: runtime-type
        text: When the component type is only known at runtime, for example from configuration or a CMS
        correct: true
      - text: To load components from JavaScript
      - text: To generate components from SQL tables
    explanation: "`DynamicComponent` takes a `Type` and a `Parameters` dictionary and renders that component."
  - id: boundary
    prompt: What does an `ErrorBoundary` do?
    options:
      - text: Prevents all exceptions in the app, including in background services
      - text: Logs exceptions to the browser console only
      - id: contain
        text: Catches unhandled exceptions thrown while rendering its child content and shows fallback UI instead of breaking the whole app
        correct: true
    explanation: Error boundaries contain rendering and lifecycle failures in a subtree. In Interactive Server, an unhandled exception without a boundary terminates the circuit.
  - id: recover
    prompt: How do you let users retry after an `ErrorBoundary` shows its error content?
    options:
      - text: Reload the page; there is no other way
      - id: recover-method
        text: Call the boundary's `Recover()` method, for example from a button or when navigating
        correct: true
      - text: Set `IsFixed` to false
    explanation: "`Recover()` resets the boundary and re-renders its child content."
---
## Learning objectives

- Render components chosen at runtime
- Contain failures with error boundaries

## DynamicComponent

```razor
@foreach (var widget in dashboard.Widgets)
{
    <DynamicComponent Type="@WidgetTypes[widget.Kind]" Parameters="@widget.Settings" />
}

@code {
    private static readonly Dictionary<string, Type> WidgetTypes = new()
    {
        ["sales"] = typeof(SalesChart),
        ["tasks"] = typeof(TaskList),
        ["weather"] = typeof(WeatherCard)
    };
}
```

`Parameters` is an `IDictionary<string, object>` whose keys must match the target component's
parameter names. Map from configuration through an allow-list like the dictionary above; never
resolve arbitrary type names from user input.

## Error boundaries

```razor
<ErrorBoundary @ref="boundary">
    <ChildContent>
        <OrderHistory CustomerId="customerId" />
    </ChildContent>
    <ErrorContent Context="ex">
        <div class="alert">
            <p>We couldn't load your orders.</p>
            <button @onclick="() => boundary?.Recover()">Try again</button>
        </div>
    </ErrorContent>
</ErrorBoundary>

@code {
    private ErrorBoundary? boundary;
}
```

Put boundaries around independent regions — a widget, a panel — so one failure does not take
down the page. A common pattern is a boundary in the main layout that calls `Recover()` whenever
the route changes:

```csharp
protected override void OnParametersSet() => boundary?.Recover();
```

## What boundaries do not catch

Exceptions in event handlers you `await` inside the component are caught, but exceptions in
fire-and-forget tasks, timers or background services are not. Handle those explicitly and log them.

## Learning objectives

- Build forms with `EditForm` and input components
- Validate with DataAnnotations
- Customise validation and keep it secure

## A complete form

```csharp
public sealed class SignupModel
{
    [Required, EmailAddress]
    public string Email { get; set; } = "";

    [Required, StringLength(64, MinimumLength = 12, ErrorMessage = "Use at least 12 characters.")]
    public string Password { get; set; } = "";

    [Range(typeof(bool), "true", "true", ErrorMessage = "Please accept the terms.")]
    public bool AcceptTerms { get; set; }
}
```

```razor
<EditForm Model="model" OnValidSubmit="SubmitAsync">
    <DataAnnotationsValidator />
    <ValidationSummary />

    <label>
        E-mail
        <InputText @bind-Value="model.Email" type="email" autocomplete="email" />
    </label>
    <ValidationMessage For="() => model.Email" />

    <label>
        Password
        <InputText @bind-Value="model.Password" type="password" autocomplete="new-password" />
    </label>
    <ValidationMessage For="() => model.Password" />

    <label><InputCheckbox @bind-Value="model.AcceptTerms" /> I accept the terms</label>

    <button type="submit" disabled="@busy">Sign up</button>
</EditForm>

@code {
    private readonly SignupModel model = new();
    private bool busy;

    private async Task SubmitAsync()
    {
        busy = true;
        try { await Accounts.SignupAsync(model); }
        finally { busy = false; }
    }
}
```

## EditContext

`EditForm` creates an `EditContext` that tracks field changes and validation messages. Use it
directly for advanced scenarios:

```csharp
private EditContext? editContext;
protected override void OnInitialized() => editContext = new EditContext(model);
private bool CanSubmit => editContext?.IsModified() == true && editContext.GetValidationMessages().Any() == false;
```

## Custom validation

Implement `IValidatableObject` for cross-field rules, or a `ValidationAttribute` for reusable rules.
For complex rule sets, libraries such as FluentValidation integrate through a custom validator
component that adds messages to a `ValidationMessageStore`.

## Security reminder

In WebAssembly and Auto apps, component code is downloaded to the browser and can be modified.
Always validate again on the server — sharing the same model class between client and API makes
that cheap.

title: Forms with static server rendering
questions:
  - id: formname
    prompt: Why does an `EditForm` in a statically rendered component need a `FormName`?

        correct: true

  - id: supply

    options:

        correct: true

    explanation: The model property is bound from the form data on POST. Initialise it with `Model ??= new()` so GET requests still have an instance.
  - id: antiforgery
    prompt: Which statements about antiforgery in Blazor Web Apps are true?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: "`EditForm` renders an antiforgery token automatically"
        correct: true

Static SSR pages have no live connection, yet forms still work — they post back to the server,
just like classic web apps, with Blazor handling binding and validation.

## Learning objectives

- Build forms that work without interactivity
- Bind posted data with `[SupplyParameterFromForm]`
- Use enhanced form posts for a smoother experience

## A static SSR form

```razor
@page "/contact"
@inject IContactService Contacts

<EditForm Model="Model" FormName="contact" OnValidSubmit="SubmitAsync" Enhance>
    <DataAnnotationsValidator />
    <InputText @bind-Value="Model!.Name" placeholder="Name" />
    <ValidationMessage For="() => Model!.Name" />
    <InputTextArea @bind-Value="Model!.Message" />
    <button type="submit">Send</button>
</EditForm>

@if (sent)
{
    <p role="status">Thanks! We'll be in touch.</p>
}

@code {
    [SupplyParameterFromForm] private ContactModel? Model { get; set; }
    private bool sent;

    protected override void OnInitialized() => Model ??= new();

    private async Task SubmitAsync()
    {
        await Contacts.SendAsync(Model!);
        sent = true;
    }
}
```

On GET, `Model` is null and gets a fresh instance. On POST, Blazor binds the form fields into
`Model`, validates, and calls `OnValidSubmit`. No WebSocket and no WebAssembly are involved.

## Enhanced form handling

The `Enhance` parameter (or `data-enhance` on a plain `<form>`) makes `blazor.web.js` submit with
`fetch` and patch the page in place instead of a full reload — scroll position and unchanged DOM
are preserved.

## Plain HTML forms

```razor
<form method="post" @onsubmit="Subscribe" @formname="newsletter" data-enhance>
    <AntiforgeryToken />
    <input name="Email" type="email" />
    <button>Subscribe</button>
</form>

@code {
    [SupplyParameterFromForm(FormName = "newsletter")] private string? Email { get; set; }
    private Task Subscribe() => Newsletter.AddAsync(Email);
}
```

## When to choose static forms

Static forms are ideal for content sites, sign-in pages, contact forms and checkout steps: they
are fast, work before (or without) WebAssembly loads, and keep the server load low because no
circuit is held open.

## Route templates

```razor
@page "/products"
@page "/products/{Category}"
@page "/products/{Category}/{Id:int}"
@page "/files/{*Path}"
```

| Feature | Example |
|---------|---------|
| Parameter | `{Category}` → `[Parameter] public string? Category { get; set; }` |
| Constraint | `{Id:int}`, `{Date:datetime}`, `{Id:guid}`, `{Active:bool}` |
| Optional | `{Page:int?}` |
| Catch-all | `{*Path}` |

## Query strings

```razor
@page "/search"

@code {
    [SupplyParameterFromQuery(Name = "q")] public string? Query { get; set; }
    [SupplyParameterFromQuery] public int? Page { get; set; }
}
```

```csharp
var url = Navigation.GetUriWithQueryParameters(new Dictionary<string, object?>
{
    ["q"] = query,
    ["page"] = 2
});
Navigation.NavigateTo(url);
```

## Navigation

```razor
<NavLink href="orders" Match="NavLinkMatch.Prefix" ActiveClass="active">Orders</NavLink>
```

```csharp
Navigation.NavigateTo("/orders/42");
Navigation.NavigateTo("/login", forceLoad: true);    // full page load
Navigation.NavigateTo("/step-2", replace: true);     // replace history entry
```

## Not found (.NET 10)

```razor
<Router AppAssembly="typeof(Program).Assembly" NotFoundPage="typeof(Pages.NotFound)">
    <Found Context="routeData">
        <RouteView RouteData="routeData" DefaultLayout="typeof(Layout.MainLayout)" />
        <FocusOnNavigate RouteData="routeData" Selector="h1" />
    </Found>
</Router>
```

```csharp
protected override async Task OnInitializedAsync()
{
    product = await Catalog.FindAsync(Id);
    if (product is null) Navigation.NotFound();
}
```

During static SSR this sets a 404 status code; in interactive modes it renders the not-found page.
`FocusOnNavigate` moves focus to the page heading after navigation, which helps screen-reader users.

## Learning objectives

- Understand enhanced navigation and how to opt out
- Use streaming rendering for slow data
- Preserve DOM regions across navigations

## Enhanced navigation

With `blazor.web.js` on the page, clicking an internal link triggers a `fetch` of the next page,
and Blazor patches the differences into the current DOM. The result feels like a single-page app,
while every page remains server-rendered HTML that search engines and no-JavaScript browsers can use.

```html
<a href="reports/export.csv" data-enhance-nav="false">Download CSV</a>
```

## Preserving regions

```html
<div data-permanent id="chat-widget">…</div>
```

Content marked `data-permanent` is left untouched by enhanced page updates — useful for
third-party widgets that keep their own state.

## Streaming rendering

```razor
@page "/weather"
@attribute [StreamRendering]

@if (forecasts is null)
{
    <p><em>Loading…</em></p>
}
else
{
    <table>
        @foreach (var f in forecasts)
        {
            <tr><td>@f.Date</td><td>@f.TemperatureC °C</td></tr>
        }
    </table>
}

@code {
    private WeatherForecast[]? forecasts;

    protected override async Task OnInitializedAsync() =>
        forecasts = await Weather.GetForecastsAsync();
}
```

The server sends the page with "Loading…" immediately and keeps the response open. When
`OnInitializedAsync` completes, it streams the updated markup, and `blazor.web.js` swaps it in.

## Choosing the right tool

| Need | Use |
|------|-----|
| Fast pages, mostly content | Static SSR + enhanced navigation |
| Slow data on a static page | `[StreamRendering]` |
| Rich interaction (drag, live updates) | An interactive render mode for that component |

## Learning objectives

- Design components that load data in any render mode
- Use `IDbContextFactory` in Interactive Server
- Call APIs from WebAssembly with `HttpClient`

## The abstraction

```csharp
// Shared (e.g. Shop.Client or a Contracts library)
public interface IProductService
{
    Task<IReadOnlyList<ProductDto>> ListAsync(string? category, CancellationToken ct = default);
}
```

```csharp
// Server project
public sealed class ServerProductService(IDbContextFactory<ShopDbContext> factory) : IProductService
{
    public async Task<IReadOnlyList<ProductDto>> ListAsync(string? category, CancellationToken ct = default)
    {
        await using var db = await factory.CreateDbContextAsync(ct);
        return await db.Products
            .AsNoTracking()
            .Where(p => category == null || p.Category == category)
            .Select(p => new ProductDto(p.Id, p.Name, p.Price))
            .ToListAsync(ct);
    }
}
```

```csharp
// Client project
public sealed class HttpProductService(HttpClient http) : IProductService
{
    public async Task<IReadOnlyList<ProductDto>> ListAsync(string? category, CancellationToken ct = default) =>
        await http.GetFromJsonAsync<List<ProductDto>>($"api/products?category={Uri.EscapeDataString(category ?? "")}", ct) ?? [];
}
```

## Registration in each host

```csharp
// Server Program.cs
builder.Services.AddDbContextFactory<ShopDbContext>(o => o.UseSqlServer(connectionString));
builder.Services.AddScoped<IProductService, ServerProductService>();
app.MapGet("/api/products", (string? category, IProductService products, CancellationToken ct) =>
    products.ListAsync(category, ct));

// Client Program.cs
builder.Services.AddScoped(sp => new HttpClient { BaseAddress = new Uri(builder.HostEnvironment.BaseAddress) });
builder.Services.AddScoped<IProductService, HttpProductService>();
```

## The component

```razor
@inject IProductService Products

@foreach (var p in products)
{
    <ProductCard Product="p" />
}

@code {
    [SupplyParameterFromQuery] public string? Category { get; set; }
    private IReadOnlyList<ProductDto> products = [];

    protected override async Task OnParametersSetAsync() =>
        products = await Products.ListAsync(Category);
}
```

This is dependency inversion in practice: the component is reusable in every render mode — and in
a Hybrid app — because it never knows where its data comes from.

title: Persisting prerendered state
questions:
  - id: double-load
    prompt: Why might an interactive component with prerendering load its data twice?
    options:
      - id: twice
        text: The component initialises once during server prerendering and again when it becomes interactive, losing the first result
        correct: true
      - text: Because of a bug in `HttpClient`
      - text: Because `OnInitializedAsync` is never called
      - text: Because the browser refreshes automatically
    explanation: Without persisted state, the interactive instance starts from scratch and repeats the work, often causing a visible flicker.
  - id: persistent-state
    prompt: In .NET 10, what is the simplest way to carry prerendered data into the interactive component?
    options:
      - text: Store it in a static field
      - text: Write it to a cookie manually
      - id: attribute
        text: Mark a public property with `[PersistentState]`
        correct: true
    explanation: The framework serializes the property into the page during prerender and restores it when the component becomes interactive.
  - id: facts
    prompt: Which statements about persistent component state are true?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: The persisted data is embedded in the HTML sent to the browser, so it must not contain secrets
        correct: true
      - text: Earlier versions used the `PersistentComponentState` service with `RegisterOnPersisting` and `TryTakeFromJson`
        correct: true
      - text: Persisted values must be JSON-serializable
        correct: true
      - text: Persisted state survives a full browser refresh forever
    explanation: The state transfers once from prerender to interactive; it is not long-term storage.
---
## Learning objectives

- Explain why prerendering can cause double data loading
- Persist state with `[PersistentState]` (.NET 10)
- Use the lower-level `PersistentComponentState` service

## The problem

1. Server prerenders the page — `OnInitializedAsync` loads products, HTML is sent
2. The component starts interactively (circuit or WebAssembly) — a new instance runs
   `OnInitializedAsync` again, momentarily shows "Loading…", then reloads the products

## Declarative persistence (.NET 10)

```razor
@inject IProductService Products

@code {
    [PersistentState]
    public List<ProductDto>? Items { get; set; }

    protected override async Task OnInitializedAsync()
    {
        Items ??= [.. await Products.ListAsync(category: null)];
    }
}
```

During prerendering the property is serialized into the page. When the interactive instance
starts, the framework restores `Items` before `OnInitializedAsync` runs, so `??=` skips the second load.

## The underlying service

```razor
@implements IDisposable
@inject PersistentComponentState AppState

@code {
    private List<ProductDto>? items;
    private PersistingComponentStateSubscription subscription;

    protected override async Task OnInitializedAsync()
    {
        subscription = AppState.RegisterOnPersisting(() =>
        {
            AppState.PersistAsJson("products", items);
            return Task.CompletedTask;
        });

        if (!AppState.TryTakeFromJson<List<ProductDto>>("products", out items))
        {
            items = [.. await Products.ListAsync(category: null)];
        }
    }

    public void Dispose() => subscription.Dispose();
}
```

## Guidelines

- Persist only what is needed to render, and never secrets — it is visible in page source
- Keep payloads small; they add to the HTML size
- Alternatively, disable prerendering for components where it adds little value

## Learning objectives

- Call JavaScript modules from components
- Call .NET from JavaScript
- Wrap browser storage in a resilient service

## Collocated modules

```javascript
// Components/CopyButton.razor.js
export function copy(text) {
  return navigator.clipboard.writeText(text);
}
```

```razor
@implements IAsyncDisposable
@inject IJSRuntime JS

<button @onclick="CopyAsync">Copy</button>

@code {
    [Parameter, EditorRequired] public string Text { get; set; } = "";
    private IJSObjectReference? module;

    protected override async Task OnAfterRenderAsync(bool firstRender)
    {
        if (firstRender)
            module = await JS.InvokeAsync<IJSObjectReference>("import", "./Components/CopyButton.razor.js");
    }

    private async Task CopyAsync()
    {
        if (module is not null) await module.InvokeVoidAsync("copy", Text);
    }

    public async ValueTask DisposeAsync()
    {
        try { if (module is not null) await module.DisposeAsync(); }
        catch (JSDisconnectedException) { }
    }
}
```

`JSDisconnectedException` occurs in Interactive Server when the circuit is gone — the browser has
already cleaned up, so it is safe to ignore during disposal.

## Calling .NET from JavaScript

```csharp
private DotNetObjectReference<Map>? selfRef;

protected override async Task OnAfterRenderAsync(bool firstRender)
{
    if (!firstRender) return;
    selfRef = DotNetObjectReference.Create(this);
    module = await JS.InvokeAsync<IJSObjectReference>("import", "./Components/Map.razor.js");
    await module.InvokeVoidAsync("init", mapElement, selfRef);
}

[JSInvokable]
public Task OnMarkerClicked(int id) => SelectAsync(id);
```

```javascript
export function init(element, dotNet) {
  element.addEventListener('marker-click', e => dotNet.invokeMethodAsync('OnMarkerClicked', e.detail.id));
}
```

## A resilient storage service

```csharp
public sealed class BrowserStorage(IJSRuntime js, ILogger<BrowserStorage> logger)
{
    public async ValueTask<T?> GetAsync<T>(string key)
    {
        try
        {
            var json = await js.InvokeAsync<string?>("localStorage.getItem", key);
            return json is null ? default : JsonSerializer.Deserialize<T>(json);
        }
        catch (Exception ex) when (ex is JSException or JsonException or InvalidOperationException)
        {
            logger.LogWarning(ex, "Could not read {Key} from local storage", key);
            return default;
        }
    }
}
```

Storage can be disabled, full or unavailable during prerendering (`InvalidOperationException`).
Fail soft: the app should keep working with in-memory state. For larger or structured data,
IndexedDB is a better fit than `localStorage` — this site stores reading progress there.

## WebAssembly-only: JSImport/JSExport

In WebAssembly, `[JSImport]` and `[JSExport]` from `System.Runtime.InteropServices.JavaScript`
offer faster, source-generated interop. They do not work in Interactive Server, so prefer
`IJSRuntime` in components that may run in either mode.

## Setup

```csharp
builder.Services.AddCascadingAuthenticationState();
builder.Services.AddAuthorization(o =>
    o.AddPolicy("catalog-admin", p => p.RequireRole("Admin").RequireClaim("department", "catalog")));
```

## In components

```razor
@page "/admin/products"
@attribute [Authorize(Policy = "catalog-admin")]

<AuthorizeView Roles="Admin">
    <Authorized>
        <p>Signed in as @context.User.Identity?.Name</p>
        <button @onclick="DeleteAsync">Delete</button>
    </Authorized>
    <NotAuthorized>
        <a href="account/login">Sign in</a>
    </NotAuthorized>
</AuthorizeView>
```

```csharp
[CascadingParameter] private Task<AuthenticationState>? AuthState { get; set; }

private async Task<bool> IsOwnerAsync(Order order)
{
    var user = (await AuthState!).User;
    return user.FindFirstValue(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier) == order.OwnerId;
}
```

## Trust boundaries by render mode

| Render mode | Where checks are enforced |
|-------------|---------------------------|
| Static SSR | On the server, per request — trustworthy |
| Interactive Server | On the server, in the circuit — trustworthy |
| WebAssembly / Auto (client) | In the browser — **UX only**; the API must authorize every call |

## Sharing auth state with WebAssembly

In a Blazor Web App with WebAssembly components, the server can serialize the authentication
state into the page so the client knows who is signed in (.NET 9+):

```csharp
// server
builder.Services.AddRazorComponents()
    .AddInteractiveWebAssemblyComponents()
    .AddAuthenticationStateSerialization();

// client
builder.Services.AddAuthorizationCore();
builder.Services.AddCascadingAuthenticationState();
builder.Services.AddAuthenticationStateDeserialization();
```

API calls from the client then use the same authentication cookie, and the server's minimal API
endpoints call `.RequireAuthorization()`.

- Scale Interactive Server

## Virtualization

```razor
<div style="height: 600px; overflow-y: auto">
    <Virtualize ItemsProvider="LoadRows" Context="row" ItemSize="40">
        <ItemContent><OrderRow Order="row" /></ItemContent>
        <Placeholder><div class="row-skeleton"></div></Placeholder>
    </Virtualize>
</div>

@code {
    private async ValueTask<ItemsProviderResult<OrderDto>> LoadRows(ItemsProviderRequest request)
    {
        var page = await Orders.PageAsync(request.StartIndex, request.Count, request.CancellationToken);
        return new ItemsProviderResult<OrderDto>(page.Items, page.TotalCount);
    }
}
```

## QuickGrid

`Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.QuickGrid` is a fast, minimal data grid with sorting, paging and
virtualization:

```razor
<QuickGrid Items="people" Pagination="pagination">
    <PropertyColumn Property="p => p.Name" Sortable="true" />
    <PropertyColumn Property="p => p.JoinedOn" Format="yyyy-MM-dd" Sortable="true" />
</QuickGrid>
<Paginator State="pagination" />

@code {
    private readonly PaginationState pagination = new() { ItemsPerPage = 20 };
    private IQueryable<Person> people = Enumerable.Empty<Person>().AsQueryable();
}
```

## Rendering less

- Keep component state close to where it is used, so changes re-render small subtrees
- Use `@key` on lists
- Override `ShouldRender` for expensive components with infrequent changes
- Avoid creating new delegates or objects as parameters on every render in hot paths

## WebAssembly download and startup

| Technique | Effect |
|-----------|--------|
| Trimming (on by default when publishing) | Removes unused IL |
| Compression (Brotli/gzip) and fingerprinted static assets | Smaller, cacheable downloads |
| Lazy loading (`BlazorWebAssemblyLazyLoad`) | Download feature assemblies only when needed |
| AOT compilation | Faster CPU-bound code; larger download |
| `InvariantGlobalization` | Skips culture data if you do not need it |

## Interactive Server at scale

Each circuit holds component state in server memory and keeps a WebSocket open. Use sticky
sessions when running multiple servers (or Azure SignalR Service), keep circuit state lean, and set
sensible limits for disconnected circuit retention.

## Learning objectives

- Render and interact with components in unit tests
- Provide fake services and parameters
- Know when to use bUnit versus browser tests

## A first test

```csharp
public class RatingTests : IDisposable
{
    private readonly BunitContext _ctx = new();

    [Fact]
    public void Clicking_the_third_star_raises_ValueChanged_with_3()
    {
        int? selected = null;
        var cut = _ctx.Render<Rating>(p => p
            .Add(c => c.Value, 1)
            .Add(c => c.ValueChanged, v => selected = v));

        cut.FindAll("button")[2].Click();

        Assert.Equal(3, selected);
    }

    public void Dispose() => _ctx.Dispose();
}
```

## Injecting fakes

```csharp
[Fact]
public void Shows_products_from_the_service()
{
    _ctx.Services.AddSingleton<IProductService>(new FakeProductService(
        new ProductDto(1, "Pen", 2.50m),
        new ProductDto(2, "Notebook", 4.00m)));

    var cut = _ctx.Render<ProductList>();

    cut.WaitForAssertion(() => Assert.Equal(2, cut.FindAll(".product-card").Count));
}
```

`WaitForAssertion` retries until async rendering completes or a timeout passes.

## JavaScript interop

```csharp
_ctx.JSInterop.Mode = JSRuntimeMode.Loose;          // unconfigured calls return defaults
var module = _ctx.JSInterop.SetupModule("./Components/CopyButton.razor.js");
module.SetupVoid("copy", "hello");
```

## Choosing the right test

| Test | Tool | Checks |
|------|------|--------|
| Component logic and markup | bUnit | Rendering, parameters, events, services |
| Services and handlers | xUnit | Pure C# logic |
| Full user journeys with real JS | Playwright | Browser behaviour end to end |

This site's own components are tested with bUnit on Microsoft.Testing.Platform.

## Learning objectives

- Understand how Blazor Hybrid works
- Host components in .NET MAUI and desktop apps
- Share components between web and native apps

## How it works

In a Hybrid app, Razor components run on the device's .NET runtime. The `BlazorWebView` control
uses the platform's web view (WebView2 on Windows, WKWebView on Apple platforms, Android WebView)
to display the HTML. Communication is a local in-process channel — no web server and no WebAssembly.

## .NET MAUI Blazor Hybrid

```bash
dotnet new maui-blazor -n Shop.Mobile
```

```xml
<!-- MainPage.xaml -->
<BlazorWebView HostPage="wwwroot/index.html">
    <BlazorWebView.RootComponents>
        <RootComponent Selector="#app" ComponentType="{x:Type local:Routes}" />
    </BlazorWebView.RootComponents>
</BlazorWebView>
```

```csharp
// MauiProgram.cs
builder.Services.AddMauiBlazorWebView();
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IGeolocationService, MauiGeolocationService>();
```

## Platform abstraction

```csharp
public interface IGeolocationService
{
    Task<(double Lat, double Lon)?> GetLocationAsync(CancellationToken ct);
}

public sealed class MauiGeolocationService : IGeolocationService
{
    public async Task<(double Lat, double Lon)?> GetLocationAsync(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var location = await Geolocation.Default.GetLocationAsync(new GeolocationRequest(), ct);
        return location is null ? null : (location.Latitude, location.Longitude);
    }
}
```

The web host registers a different implementation (for example, one that uses the browser
Geolocation API through JS interop). The shared component only knows `IGeolocationService`.

## The `maui-blazor-web` template

`dotnet new maui-blazor-web` creates a solution with a MAUI Hybrid app, a Blazor Web App and a
shared Razor class library already wired together — a quick start for apps that target web,
desktop and mobile from one set of components.

## Learning objectives

- Choose a hosting strategy for each Blazor model
- Deploy standalone WebAssembly to static hosting
- Operate Interactive Server reliably

## Hosting options

| App type | Host |
|----------|------|
| Blazor Web App (any render mode) | ASP.NET Core: App Service, containers, Kubernetes, IIS |
| Standalone WebAssembly | Any static host: GitHub Pages, Azure Static Web Apps, S3 + CloudFront |
| Hybrid | App stores, MSIX, installers |

## Standalone WebAssembly on GitHub Pages

```bash
dotnet publish src/MySite -c Release -o publish
```

Deploy `publish/wwwroot`. A few details matter on GitHub Pages:

- Add an empty `.nojekyll` file so folders starting with `_` (like `_framework`) are served
- Provide a fallback for deep links (a `404.html` that redirects to `index.html` with the original path)
- Set `<base href>` correctly if the site lives under a sub-path such as `/repo-name/`

This site uses exactly this setup.

## Interactive Server in production

- WebSockets enabled end to end; long-polling is a slow fallback
- Sticky sessions (ARR affinity) or Azure SignalR Service for scale-out
- Data Protection keys shared across instances (for antiforgery and auth cookies)
- Tune `CircuitOptions`, such as `DisconnectedCircuitMaxRetained` and `DisconnectedCircuitRetentionPeriod`

The .NET 10 templates include a `ReconnectModal` component with its own CSS and JavaScript, so
the reconnection experience is easy to customise.

## Observability

Blazor Server emits metrics and traces for circuits and component rendering through the standard
.NET diagnostics APIs, so the OpenTelemetry setup from any ASP.NET Core app applies here too.

## Learning objectives

- Explain what modern .NET is and how it differs from .NET Framework
- Understand the LTS/STS release and support model
- Identify the main workloads built on .NET

## One platform

Modern .NET — the line that started as .NET Core and dropped "Core" at version 5 — is an open
source, cross-platform runtime and SDK for Windows, Linux and macOS on x64 and Arm64. One base
class library serves web apps, services, desktop, mobile (.NET MAUI), cloud functions, games and
command-line tools.

.NET Framework 4.8.x still ships with Windows and is supported, but it is Windows-only and receives
no new features. New development should target modern .NET.

## Release cadence

| Version | Released | Type | Support ends |
|---------|----------|------|--------------|
| .NET 8 | Nov 2023 | LTS | Nov 2026 |
| .NET 9 | Nov 2024 | STS | Nov 2026 |
| .NET 10 | Nov 2025 | LTS | Nov 2028 |

- A major version ships every **November**
- **Even** numbers are **LTS** (3 years); **odd** numbers are **STS** (24 months since the policy
  change announced in 2025, previously 18)
- **Patch Tuesday** servicing releases ship monthly

Pick LTS for systems that upgrade rarely; STS is fine for teams that upgrade every year.

## What ships in .NET 10

- **C# 14** — extension members, the `field` keyword, null-conditional assignment and more
- **ASP.NET Core 10** — minimal API validation, OpenAPI 3.1, Blazor improvements
- **EF Core 10** — `LeftJoin`/`RightJoin` operators, named query filters, vector search for SQL
- **SDK** — file-based apps with `dotnet run app.cs`, `dotnet tool exec`, SLNX solution files
- **Runtime** — JIT, GC and AVX10.2 improvements, more Native AOT support

## Target framework monikers

```xml
<TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
<!-- or several -->
<TargetFrameworks>net8.0;net10.0</TargetFrameworks>
```

Platform-specific TFMs add a suffix: `net10.0-windows`, `net10.0-android`, `net10.0-ios`.

## Learning objectives

- Use the core `dotnet` CLI commands
- Pin SDK versions with `global.json`
- Write file-based apps for scripts and prototypes

## Everyday commands

```bash
dotnet new list                         # available templates
dotnet new sln -n Shop                  # .NET 10 creates Shop.slnx by default
dotnet new webapi -n Shop.Api
dotnet sln add Shop.Api
dotnet add Shop.Api package Dapper
dotnet build
dotnet test
dotnet run --project Shop.Api
dotnet publish Shop.Api -c Release -o ./out
```

`build`, `run`, `test` and `publish` perform an implicit `restore`.

## Pinning the SDK

```json
{
  "sdk": {
    "version": "10.0.100",
    "rollForward": "latestFeature"
  }
}
```

`rollForward: latestFeature` accepts a newer feature band or patch of 10.0 but never jumps to 11.

## SLNX solution files

The XML-based `.slnx` format replaces the old `.sln` format with something humans can read and
merge. `dotnet sln migrate` converts an existing solution.

```xml
<Solution>
  <Folder Name="/src/">
    <Project Path="src/Shop.Api/Shop.Api.csproj" />
  </Folder>
  <Folder Name="/tests/">
    <Project Path="tests/Shop.Api.Tests/Shop.Api.Tests.csproj" />
  </Folder>
</Solution>
```

## File-based apps

.NET 10 can run a single file directly:

```csharp
#!/usr/bin/env dotnet
#:package Humanizer@2.14.1

using Humanizer;

var released = new DateTime(2025, 11, 11);
Console.WriteLine($".NET 10 shipped {(DateTime.Now - released).Humanize()} ago.");
```

```bash
dotnet run released.cs
```

Directives such as `#:package`, `#:sdk` and `#:property` replace the project file. When a script
outgrows one file, `dotnet project convert released.cs` turns it into a regular project.

## Tools

```bash
dotnet tool install --global dotnet-ef
dotnet tool exec dotnet-outdated-tool   # run a tool once without installing it (new in .NET 10)
dnx dotnet-outdated-tool                # shorthand for the same thing
```

## Learning objectives

- Read and write SDK-style project files
- Share settings with `Directory.Build.props`
- Manage package versions centrally

## A minimal project

```xml
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>
```

All `.cs` files below the folder are compiled. `ImplicitUsings` adds common `global using`
directives (`System`, `System.Linq`, `System.Threading.Tasks`, and web namespaces for the Web SDK).

## Shared settings

`Directory.Build.props` at the repository root is imported into every project:

```xml
<Project>
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <LangVersion>latest</LangVersion>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>
    <AnalysisLevel>latest-recommended</AnalysisLevel>
    <ManagePackageVersionsCentrally>true</ManagePackageVersionsCentrally>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>
```

## Central package management

```xml
<!-- Directory.Packages.props -->
<Project>
  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageVersion Include="Dapper" Version="2.1.66" />
    <PackageVersion Include="xunit.v3" Version="4.0.2" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>
```

```xml
<!-- a project file -->
<ItemGroup>
  <PackageReference Include="Dapper" />
</ItemGroup>
```

One version per package across the repo eliminates "works in project A, breaks in project B"
drift. Use `VersionOverride` on a `PackageReference` only for deliberate exceptions.

## Quality gates in the build

- `TreatWarningsAsErrors` — warnings cannot accumulate
- `Nullable` — null-safety analysis
- `AnalysisLevel` — enable more .NET analyzers
- `EnforceCodeStyleInBuild` — make `.editorconfig` style rules part of the build

> Treat the build as your first reviewer. Every rule it enforces is a comment nobody has to write.

## Learning objectives

- Choose between classes, structs and records
- Use primary constructors and `required` members
- Write expressive logic with pattern matching

## Records

```csharp
public sealed record Product(string Sku, string Name, decimal Price);

var a = new Product("B-1", "Book", 12m);
var b = a with { Price = 10m };   // non-destructive mutation
Console.WriteLine(a == b);        // False
Console.WriteLine(a);             // Product { Sku = B-1, Name = Book, Price = 12 }
```

Positional records generate `init`-only properties, a deconstructor, value equality and a readable
`ToString`. `record struct` gives the same features for value types.

## Primary constructors

```csharp
public sealed class OrderService(IOrderRepository orders, TimeProvider time, ILogger<OrderService> logger)
{
    public async Task<Order> PlaceAsync(Cart cart, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var order = Order.From(cart, time.GetUtcNow());
        await orders.AddAsync(order, ct);
        logger.LogInformation("Placed order {OrderId}", order.Id);
        return order;
    }
}
```

The parameters are captured, not exposed. They are mutable, so if immutability matters, assign
them to `readonly` fields.

## Required members

```csharp
public sealed class SmtpOptions
{
    public required string Host { get; init; }
    public int Port { get; init; } = 587;
}
```

## Pattern matching

```csharp
static decimal ShippingCost(Order order) => order switch
{
    { Total: >= 100m } => 0m,
    { Destination.Country: "US", Weight: < 1.0 } => 4.99m,
    { Destination.Country: "US" } => 9.99m,
    { IsExpress: true } => 29.99m,
    _ => 19.99m
};

static string Describe(int[] values) => values switch
{
    [] => "empty",
    [var only] => $"one item: {only}",
    [var first, .., var last] => $"from {first} to {last}"
};
```

The compiler warns when a switch expression is not exhaustive, turning missing cases into build
feedback rather than runtime surprises.

- Use the `field` keyword

## The `field` keyword

```csharp
public sealed class Customer
{
    public string Name
    {
        get;
        set => field = value?.Trim() ?? throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(value));
    }
}
```

Before C# 14 you needed a private `_name` field just to add the trimming logic.

## Extension members

```csharp
public static class EnumerableExtensions
{
    extension<T>(IEnumerable<T> source)
    {
        public bool IsEmpty => !source.Any();

        public IEnumerable<T> WhereNotNull() => source.Where(x => x is not null);
    }

    extension<T>(IEnumerable<T>)
    {
        public static IEnumerable<T> Empty => [];
    }
}

var names = new[] { "Ada", "Grace" };
Console.WriteLine(names.IsEmpty);                 // extension property
var none = IEnumerable<string>.Empty;             // static extension member
```

Classic `this`-parameter extension methods still work and are source- and binary-compatible.

## Null-conditional assignment


## Smaller improvements

```csharp
Console.WriteLine(nameof(Dictionary<,>));         // "Dictionary"
```

- **Partial constructors and events** — useful for source generators
- **User-defined compound assignment operators** — types can define `operator +=` to update in place
  instead of allocating a new instance

## Learning objectives

- Use collection expressions
- Understand deferred execution
- Use the newest LINQ operators and the right collection type

## Collection expressions

```csharp
int[] primes = [2, 3, 5, 7];
List<string> names = ["Ada", "Grace"];
ReadOnlySpan<byte> header = [0x89, 0x50, 0x4E, 0x47];
IReadOnlyList<int> empty = [];
int[] combined = [..primes, 11, 13];
```

The target type decides what is created, so `[]` replaces `new List<T>()`, `Array.Empty<T>()` and
friends.

## Deferred execution

```csharp
var query = orders.Where(o => o.Total > 100);   // nothing runs yet
orders.Add(new Order(Total: 500));
var count = query.Count();                       // includes the new order
var snapshot = query.ToList();                   // materialise once, reuse
```

Materialise with `ToList()`/`ToArray()` when you will enumerate more than once, or when the source
may change.

## Newer operators

```csharp
var wordsByLength = words.CountBy(w => w.Length);            // .NET 9
var totals = orders.AggregateBy(o => o.CustomerId, 0m, (sum, o) => sum + o.Total);
foreach (var (index, item) in items.Index()) { }             // .NET 9

var withOrders = customers.LeftJoin(                          // .NET 10
    orders,
    c => c.Id,
    o => o.CustomerId,
    (c, o) => new { c.Name, OrderId = o?.Id });
```

Before .NET 10, a left join needed `GroupJoin` plus `SelectMany` plus `DefaultIfEmpty`.

## Choosing collections

| Need | Type |
|------|------|
| Ordered, indexable, growable | `List<T>` |
| Fast key lookup | `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` |
| Uniqueness | `HashSet<T>` |
| Read-only lookup built once | `FrozenDictionary`, `FrozenSet` |
| Thread-safe shared state | `ConcurrentDictionary<TKey, TValue>` |
| Expose without allowing mutation | `IReadOnlyList<T>`, `IReadOnlyDictionary<TKey, TValue>` |
| Priority-based processing | `PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority>` |

```csharp
private static readonly FrozenDictionary<string, decimal> VatRates =
    new Dictionary<string, decimal> { ["DE"] = 0.19m, ["FR"] = 0.20m }.ToFrozenDictionary();
```

title: Async and await done right
questions:
  - id: thread
    prompt: While an `await` on an I/O operation (such as an HTTP call) is pending, what happens to the thread that started it?
    options:
      - text: It is blocked until the operation completes
      - text: It is terminated
      - id: released
        text: It is released to do other work; a thread resumes the method when the operation completes
        correct: true
      - text: It spins in a loop checking for completion
    explanation: Async I/O frees threads while waiting, which is why async code scales better under load.
  - id: blocking

    options:

        correct: true

      - text: They return the wrong value
    explanation: Blocking on async code wastes threads, and in environments with a synchronization context it can deadlock. Use `await` all the way up.
  - id: async-void
    prompt: When is `async void` appropriate?
    options:

      - id: handlers

        correct: true

    explanation: Exceptions from `async void` cannot be caught by the caller and crash the process. Return `Task` everywhere else.

    type: multiple

        correct: true

        correct: true
      - text: Use `CancellationTokenSource.CancelAfter` or a linked source to impose timeouts
        correct: true

    explanation: Flow tokens end-to-end and let cancellation surface as `OperationCanceledException`, which frameworks treat as a cancelled request rather than a failure.

## Learning objectives

- Explain what `await` does and does not do
- Avoid blocking, `async void` and other common mistakes
- Flow cancellation through an application

## What await does

`await` does not create threads. It registers a continuation and returns control to the caller.
For I/O-bound work — HTTP, databases, files — no thread is consumed while waiting.

```csharp
public async Task<WeatherForecast?> GetForecastAsync(string city, CancellationToken ct)
{
    using var response = await _http.GetAsync($"forecast/{Uri.EscapeDataString(city)}", ct);
    if (response.StatusCode == HttpStatusCode.NotFound) return null;
    response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
    return await response.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<WeatherForecast>(ct);
}
```

## Concurrency, not just asynchrony

```csharp
var userTask = _users.GetAsync(id, ct);
var ordersTask = _orders.ListAsync(id, ct);
await Task.WhenAll(userTask, ordersTask);
var (user, orders) = (userTask.Result, ordersTask.Result); // safe: both tasks have completed
```

Starting both before awaiting lets them run at the same time.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
|---------|-----|
| `task.Result` / `task.Wait()` on incomplete tasks | `await task` |
| `async void` methods | `async Task` (except event handlers) |
| `Task.Run` around I/O in ASP.NET Core | Call the async API directly |
| Forgetting to pass the `CancellationToken` | Thread it through every call |
| Returning `Task` from inside `using` without awaiting | `await` inside the `using` scope |

## ConfigureAwait

`ConfigureAwait(false)` tells the continuation not to resume on the captured synchronization
context. ASP.NET Core has no synchronization context, so it rarely matters in app code; library
authors often still use it because their code may run under UI frameworks.

## ValueTask

`ValueTask<T>` avoids allocating a `Task<T>` when results are often available synchronously (for
example from a cache). It has rules — never await it twice — so use it only for measured hot paths.

## Timeouts with cancellation

```csharp
using var cts = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(requestToken);
cts.CancelAfter(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5));
await _payments.ChargeAsync(amount, cts.Token);
```

## Learning objectives

- Produce and consume async streams
- Build producer/consumer pipelines with channels
- Choose between async and parallel processing

## Async streams

```csharp
public async IAsyncEnumerable<Customer> AllCustomersAsync([EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken ct = default)
{
    string? continuation = null;
    do
    {
        var page = await _api.GetCustomersAsync(continuation, ct);
        foreach (var customer in page.Items) yield return customer;
        continuation = page.Next;
    } while (continuation is not null);
}

await foreach (var customer in client.AllCustomersAsync(ct))
{
    Console.WriteLine(customer.Name);
}
```

In .NET 10, the LINQ operators for `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` (`System.Linq.AsyncEnumerable`) are
part of the base libraries, so `WhereAwait`-style helpers from third-party packages are no longer
needed.

## Channels

```csharp
var channel = Channel.CreateBounded<Order>(new BoundedChannelOptions(100)
{
    FullMode = BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait
});

var producer = Task.Run(async () =>
{
    await foreach (var order in ReadOrdersAsync(ct)) await channel.Writer.WriteAsync(order, ct);
    channel.Writer.Complete();
});

var consumer = Task.Run(async () =>
{
    await foreach (var order in channel.Reader.ReadAllAsync(ct)) await ProcessAsync(order, ct);
});

await Task.WhenAll(producer, consumer);
```

In ASP.NET Core, a channel registered as a singleton plus a `BackgroundService` reader is a
lightweight in-process work queue.

## Parallelism

```csharp
await Parallel.ForEachAsync(imageUrls, new ParallelOptions { MaxDegreeOfParallelism = 4, CancellationToken = ct },
    async (url, token) =>
    {
        var bytes = await http.GetByteArrayAsync(url, token);
        await File.WriteAllBytesAsync(Path.Combine(dir, Path.GetFileName(url)), bytes, token);
    });
```

## Locks

```csharp
private readonly Lock _gate = new();

public void Increment()
{
    lock (_gate) { _count++; }
}
```

`System.Threading.Lock` is a dedicated lock type that the compiler recognises in `lock` statements.
For simple counters, `Interlocked.Increment(ref _count)` is cheaper still.

title: Memory, spans and measuring performance

## Learning objectives

- Use `Span<T>` and `Memory<T>` to avoid copying
- Pool buffers and use `stackalloc` safely
- Measure before optimising

## The cost of allocations

Every heap allocation eventually costs garbage-collection work. On hot paths — parsers,
serializers, middleware — allocation-free code can make a large difference. Everywhere else,
clarity wins.

## Spans

```csharp
public static class Csv
{
    public static int Sum(ReadOnlySpan<char> line)
    {
        var total = 0;
        foreach (var range in line.Split(','))
        {
            total += int.Parse(line[range]);
        }
        return total;
    }
}

Console.WriteLine(Csv.Sum("1,2,3,4"));
```

`MemoryExtensions.Split` (.NET 9) enumerates ranges without creating substrings, and
`int.Parse` accepts spans directly.

| Type | Lives | Use for |
|------|-------|---------|
| `Span<T>` / `ReadOnlySpan<T>` | Stack only (`ref struct`) | Synchronous slicing and parsing |
| `Memory<T>` / `ReadOnlyMemory<T>` | Heap-storable | Async APIs, fields |

## Pooling and stackalloc

```csharp
var buffer = ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Rent(64 * 1024);
try
{
    int read;
    while ((read = await stream.ReadAsync(buffer.AsMemory(), ct)) > 0)
        hasher.AppendData(buffer.AsSpan(0, read));
}
finally
{
    ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Return(buffer);
}

Span<byte> small = stackalloc byte[16];
Random.Shared.NextBytes(small);
```

Keep `stackalloc` small (a few hundred bytes); large stack buffers risk stack overflow.

## Measure

```csharp
[MemoryDiagnoser]
public class ParsingBenchmarks
{
    private const string Line = "10,20,30,40,50";

    [Benchmark(Baseline = true)]
    public int WithSplit() => Line.Split(',').Sum(int.Parse);

    [Benchmark]
    public int WithSpan() => Csv.Sum(Line);
}
```

```bash
dotnet run -c Release
```

Optimise only what a profiler or benchmark shows is slow, and keep the readable version when the
gain does not matter.

## The host

```csharp
var builder = Host.CreateApplicationBuilder(args);
builder.Services.AddSingleton(TimeProvider.System);
builder.Services.AddHostedService<CleanupWorker>();
await builder.Build().RunAsync();
```

`WebApplication.CreateBuilder` is the same idea with the web server added. Both give you DI,
configuration, logging and graceful shutdown on Ctrl+C or SIGTERM.

## A background worker

```csharp
public sealed partial class CleanupWorker(
    IServiceScopeFactory scopes,
    TimeProvider time,
    ILogger<CleanupWorker> logger) : BackgroundService
{
    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
    {
        using var timer = new PeriodicTimer(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5), time);
        while (await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(stoppingToken))
        {
            await using var scope = scopes.CreateAsyncScope();
            var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<ShopDbContext>();
            var removed = await db.Carts
                .Where(c => c.UpdatedAt < time.GetUtcNow().AddDays(-30))
                .ExecuteDeleteAsync(stoppingToken);
            LogRemoved(removed);
        }
    }

    [LoggerMessage(Level = LogLevel.Information, Message = "Removed {Count} abandoned carts")]
    private partial void LogRemoved(int count);
}
```

## Registration patterns

```csharp
services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, SqlOrderRepository>();
services.AddSingleton<IShippingMethod, StandardShipping>();
services.AddSingleton<IShippingMethod, ExpressShipping>();      // IEnumerable<IShippingMethod> gets both
services.TryAddSingleton<IClock, SystemClock>();                // only if not already registered
services.AddKeyedSingleton<ICache, MemoryCache>("local");
services.AddKeyedSingleton<ICache, RedisCache>("distributed");
```

```csharp
public sealed class CatalogService([FromKeyedServices("distributed")] ICache cache) { }
```

## Validation

In the Development environment, ASP.NET Core enables `ValidateScopes` and `ValidateOnBuild`, so
captive dependencies and missing registrations fail at startup. You can enable them for any host:

```csharp
builder.ConfigureContainer(new DefaultServiceProviderFactory(new ServiceProviderOptions
{
    ValidateScopes = true,
    ValidateOnBuild = true
}));
```
